paragraphs: That was how Fetyukovitch finished, and the audience’s enthusiasm broke out like a storm nobody could hold back. Stopping it was out of the question. The women wept, and so did many of the men. Even two important personages had tears on their faces. The President gave way and did not even ring his bell for a while. To put down such enthusiasm, as the ladies cried afterwards, would have been to put down something sacred. The speaker himself was genuinely touched.

And it was just then that Ippolit Kirillovitch got to his feet to raise some objections. People stared at him with hatred. “What? What does this mean? He actually has the nerve to object!” the ladies babbled. But if every lady in the world, his own wife among them, had protested, nothing could have held him back at that moment. He was pale and trembling with emotion. His first phrases were not even understandable. He gasped for breath, could hardly speak plainly and lost his thread. Soon, though, he pulled himself together. Of this second speech I will quote only a few sentences.

“... I am accused of having spun a romance. But what is this defense if not one romance heaped on another? The only thing missing was poetry. Fyodor Pavlovitch, as he waits for his mistress, rips open the envelope and flings it on the floor. We are even told what he said as he did this odd thing. Is that not a flight of fancy? And what proof do we have that he had taken the money out? Who heard what he said? The feeble-minded idiot Smerdyakov, made over into a Byronic hero who takes revenge on society for his illegitimate birth—is that not a romance in the Byronic style? And the son who bursts into his father’s house and murders him without murdering him is not even a romance. He is a sphinx that sets us a riddle he cannot solve himself. If he murdered him, he murdered him. What is the meaning of murdering him without having murdered him? Who can make head or tail of that?

“Next we are lectured that our tribune is a tribune of true and sound ideas, and from this tribune of ‘sound ideas’ a solemn declaration is made that calling the murder of a father ‘parricide’ is nothing but a prejudice! But if parricide is a prejudice, and if every child is to ask his father why he should love him, what will become of us? What will become of the foundations of society? What will become of the family? Parricide, it seems, is only a bogy for Moscow merchants’ wives. The most precious and most sacred guarantees for the destiny and future of Russian justice are laid before us in a twisted and frivolous form, all to reach a single aim—to justify something that cannot be justified. ‘Oh, crush him with mercy,’ cries the counsel for the defense. But mercy is all the criminal wants, and tomorrow we will see how crushed he is. And is the counsel for the defense not too modest in asking only that the prisoner be acquitted? Why not found a charity in honor of the parricide, to keep his exploit in memory for generations to come? Religion and the Gospel are corrected—all that is mysticism, we are told, and ours is the only true Christianity, the one that has been put to the test of reason and common sense. And so a false image of Christ is set up before us! ‘With the measure you use, it shall be measured to you again,’ cried the counsel for the defense, and he instantly concludes that Christ teaches us to measure as it is measured to us—and this from the tribune of truth and sound sense! We look into the Gospel only on the eve of making speeches, to dazzle the audience with our acquaintance with a book that is, at any rate, a rather original composition, and may be useful for creating a certain effect—all to serve our purpose! But what Christ commands us is something very different. He bids us beware of doing this, because the wicked world does it. We ought to forgive and to turn the other cheek, and not to measure out to our persecutors what they measure out to us. This is what our God has taught us. He did not teach us that forbidding children to murder their fathers is a prejudice. And we will not, from the tribune of truth and good sense, correct the Gospel of our Lord, Whom the counsel for the defense condescends to call only ‘the crucified lover of humanity,’ in defiance of all orthodox Russia, which cries out to Him, ‘For You are our God!’”

At this the President broke in and reined in the over-eager speaker. He begged him not to exaggerate, not to go beyond the proper limits, and so on, the way presidents always do in such cases. The audience was uneasy too. The public was restless, and there were even shouts of indignation. Fetyukovitch hardly answered at all. He only stepped up to the tribune, laid his hand on his heart and, in an offended voice, spoke a few dignified words. Once more he touched lightly and ironically on “romancing” and “psychology,” and at a fitting moment he quoted, “Jupiter, you are angry, therefore you are wrong.” This drew a burst of approving laughter from the audience, since Ippolit Kirillovitch was nothing like Jupiter. Next, _à propos_ of the charge that he was teaching the young generation to murder their fathers, Fetyukovitch declared with great dignity that he would not even reply. As for the prosecutor’s accusation of unorthodox opinions, Fetyukovitch hinted that this was a personal insinuation. He had expected, he said, to be safe in this court from charges “damaging to my reputation as a citizen and a loyal subject.” At those words the President stopped him as well, and Fetyukovitch ended with a bow, to a murmur of approval through the courtroom. And Ippolit Kirillovitch was, in the view of our ladies, “finished for good.”

After that, the prisoner was given leave to speak. Mitya rose, but he said very little. He was dreadfully worn out, in body and in spirit. The strong, independent look he had worn on coming in that morning was almost gone. He seemed to have lived through something that day which had taught him, for the rest of his life, a very important lesson he had never grasped before. His voice was feeble, and he no longer shouted. His words carried a new note of humility, defeat and surrender.

“What can I say, gentlemen of the jury? The hour of judgment has come for me. I feel God’s hand on me! This is the end of a man who has gone astray! But I tell you again, before God, I am innocent of my father’s blood! For the last time I say it: I did not kill him! I went astray, but I loved what is good. Every moment I tried to reform, and yet I lived like a wild beast. I thank the prosecutor. He told me a great deal about myself that I didn’t know. But it’s not true that I killed my father. The prosecutor is mistaken. I thank my counsel too. I cried while I listened to him. But it’s not true that I killed my father, and he needn’t have supposed it. And don’t believe the doctors. I am perfectly sane; it’s only that my heart is heavy. If you spare me, if you let me go, I will pray for you. I will be a better man. I give you my word before God, I will! And if you condemn me, I’ll break my sword over my own head myself and kiss the pieces. But spare me, don’t rob me of my God! I know myself, I will rebel! My heart is heavy, gentlemen ... spare me!”
He nearly dropped back into his seat. His voice cracked, and he could barely get out the last words. Then the judges moved on to the questions and began asking both sides to state their conclusions.

But I will not go into the details. At last the jury got up to withdraw and deliberate. The President was very tired, so his final instructions to the jury were rather weak. “Be impartial. Do not let the eloquence of the defense sway you, but weigh the arguments nonetheless. Remember that a heavy responsibility rests on you,” and so on and so forth.

The jury went out and the court adjourned. People could stand up, walk about, trade the impressions they had stored up, and get refreshments at the buffet. It was very late, nearly one in the morning, but nobody left. The tension was so great that nobody could think of rest. Everyone waited with a sinking heart—though perhaps that goes too far, since the ladies were merely hysterically impatient, and their hearts were quite calm. An acquittal, they felt, was bound to come. They were all preparing for a dramatic moment of general rejoicing. I must admit that many of the men, too, were sure of an acquittal. Some were glad, some frowned, and some were simply downcast because they did not want him acquitted. Fetyukovitch himself was sure of his triumph. People crowded around him, congratulating him and flattering him.

“There are,” he told one group, as I heard later, “there are invisible threads that tie the counsel for the defense to the jury. During a speech one can feel them forming. I felt them. They exist. Our case is won. You can put your minds at ease.”
“What will our peasants say to all this?” asked a stout, sour-looking, pock-marked gentleman, a local landowner, as he walked up to a group of gentlemen talking together.
“But they’re not all peasants. There are four government clerks among them.”
“Yes, there are clerks,” said a member of the district council, joining the group.
“And do you know that Nazaryev, the merchant with the medal, is a juryman?”
“What about him?”
“He’s a man with brains.”
“But he never speaks.”
“He’s no great talker, but that’s all the better. The man from Petersburg has nothing to teach him. He could teach the whole of Petersburg himself. He’s the father of twelve children. Think of that!”
“Surely you don’t imagine they won’t acquit him?” one of our young officials exclaimed in another group.
“They’ll acquit him for certain,” said a firm voice.

“It would be shameful, disgraceful, not to acquit him!” cried the official. “Say he did murder him—there are fathers and fathers! Besides, he was in such a frenzy.... He may really have done nothing more than swing the pestle through the air and knock the old man down by accident. But it was a pity they dragged the valet in. That was just an absurd theory! If I’d been in Fetyukovitch’s place, I would have said it straight out: ‘He murdered him, but he isn’t guilty, hang it all!’”
“That’s just what he did, only without the ‘Hang it all!’”
“No, Mihail Semyonovitch, he very nearly said that, too,” put in a third voice.
“Why, gentlemen, in our town during Lent they acquitted an actress who had cut the throat of her lover’s lawful wife.”
“Oh, but she didn’t finish cutting it.”
“That makes no difference. She started cutting it.”
“What did you make of what he said about children? Splendid, wasn’t it?”
“Splendid!”
“And about mysticism, too!”
“Oh, enough about mysticism!” cried someone else. “Think of Ippolit and what lies ahead of him from today. His wife will scratch his eyes out tomorrow, for Mitya’s sake.”
“Is she here?”
“Whatever for? If she’d been here, she’d have scratched them out in court. She’s at home with a toothache. He he he!”
“He he he!”
In a third group:
“They’ll acquit Mitenka in the end, I expect.”
“I wouldn’t be surprised if he turns the ‘Metropolis’ upside down tomorrow. He’ll be drinking for ten days!”
“Oh, the devil!”
“The devil’s bound to have a hand in it. Where else would he be, if not here?”
“Well, gentlemen, I admit it was eloquent. But still, it’s not the thing to break your father’s head with a pestle! Or what are we coming to?”
“The chariot! Do you remember the chariot?”
“Yes, he turned a cart into a chariot!”
“And tomorrow he’ll turn a chariot into a cart, whichever suits him.”
“What cunning fellows there are these days! Is there any justice to be had in Russia?”

But then the bell rang. The jury had been out for exactly an hour, not a minute more or less. A deep silence fell over the court as soon as the public had sat down again. I remember the jurymen filing in. At last! I won’t give the questions in order; I have in fact forgotten them. I remember only the answer to the President’s first and main question: “Did the prisoner commit the murder for the sake of robbery and with premeditation?” (I don’t remember the exact words.) There was total quiet. The foreman of the jury, the youngest of the clerks, announced in a clear, loud voice, in the deathlike stillness of the court:
“Yes, guilty!”

And the same answer came back to every question: “Yes, guilty!” with not the slightest word softening it. Nobody had expected this. Almost everyone had counted on at least a recommendation to mercy. The deathlike silence in the court held—everyone seemed turned to stone, those who wanted him convicted as much as those who had longed for his acquittal. But that was only for the first instant, and then a terrible uproar broke out. Many of the men in the audience were pleased. Some rubbed their hands and made no attempt to hide their delight. Those who disagreed with the verdict looked crushed. They shrugged, they whispered, but they still seemed unable to take it in. But how am I to describe the state the ladies were in? I thought they would start a riot. At first they could hardly believe their ears. Then all at once the whole court rang with cries: “What does this mean? What next?” They jumped up from their seats. They seemed to imagine it might be reviewed and overturned on the spot. At that moment Mitya suddenly stood up and cried out in a heartbreaking voice, stretching out his hands in front of him:
“I swear by God and the dreadful Day of Judgment, I am not guilty of my father’s blood! Katya, I forgive you! Brothers, friends, take pity on the other woman!”

He could not go on. He burst into a terrible sobbing wail that was heard all over the court, in a strange, unnatural voice that was not his own. From the farthest corner at the back of the gallery came a piercing shriek—it was Grushenka. She had managed to beg her way into the court again before the lawyers began their speeches. Mitya was led away. The sentence was put off until the next day. The whole court was in an uproar, but I did not stay to hear it. I remember only a few remarks I caught on the steps as I went out.
“He’ll get a twenty-year trip to the mines!”
“Not less.”
“Well, our peasants stood firm.”
“And finished off our Mitya.”
